ACTION: Add two tests to `tests/test_export.py`. Use the reading helper that the four existing tests already use (shown here as `make_reading`). Add any missing imports (`io`, `date`, `datetime`, `timezone`) at the top.
```python
def test_since_includes_readings_on_the_boundary_day():
    readings = [
        make_reading(datetime(2026, 3, 9, 23, 59, tzinfo=timezone.utc)),
        make_reading(datetime(2026, 3, 10, 0, 0, tzinfo=timezone.utc)),
        make_reading(datetime(2026, 3, 11, 12, 0, tzinfo=timezone.utc)),
    ]
    out = io.StringIO()
    export_csv(readings, out, since=date(2026, 3, 10))

    expected = io.StringIO()
    export_csv(readings[1:], expected)
    assert out.getvalue() == expected.getvalue()


def test_without_since_writes_every_reading():
    readings = [
        make_reading(datetime(2026, 3, 9, 23, 59, tzinfo=timezone.utc)),
        make_reading(datetime(2026, 3, 10, 0, 0, tzinfo=timezone.utc)),
    ]
    out = io.StringIO()
    export_csv(readings, out)

    expected = io.StringIO()
    export_csv(readings, expected, since=date.min)
    assert out.getvalue() == expected.getvalue()
```

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The new tests compare `export_csv` with itself on a hand-picked subset. Because of this, they do not depend on the CSV column layout. A future column change will not break them.
- The boundary test uses 23:59 on the day before and 00:00 on the boundary day. Those two readings are the ones a `<` versus `<=` error, or a local-time error, would get wrong.
- I call `.astimezone(timezone.utc)` before `.date()`, even though tidelog stores UTC. This costs nothing. It also keeps the filter correct if a caller ever passes an aware datetime in a different zone.
